newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mrs. Clinton, Chelsea start 3-day visit to S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Mrs. Clinton, Chelsea start 3-day visit to S.Africa.

text.p: Hillary Rodham Clinton began a three-day visit to South Africa on Tuesday saying the country still faced many challenges in the post-apartheid period but that the United States was committed to helping.

"The solid partnership between South Africa and the United States is stronger than ever," Mrs. Clinton said in a statement issued as she and her daughter Chelsea arrived in Johannesburg after an all-night flight from the West African nation of Senegal.

During a day-long visit to Johannesburg and two days in Cape Town, President Clinton's wife said she was eager to witness first-hand the work being done to educate children, protect girls and women from violence and build a non-racial, multi-ethnic society "that will be an example to the world".
A main theme of her two-week goodwill tour of six African nations is to promote better health and education for African women and children.

After some rest at a hotel, she planned to participate in a forum at the Entandweni Lower School in the township of Soweto, lay a wreath at the Hector Peterson Memorial commemorating the anti-apartheid struggle, tour the Orlando Children's Home and join prominent women for a roundtable discussions on crime and domestic violence.
"South Africa still faces many challenges -- housing, health care, education, job creation and crime are all concerns here -- just as they are around the world," Mrs. Clinton said.
Echoing U.S. Vice President Al Gore's message from a recent visit here, Mrs. Clinton said: "America remains firmly committed to working with South Africa to address these issues."
It was the second visit by Mrs. Clinton to South Africa. She had attended the May 1994 inauguration of South African President Nelson Mandela.
During her Cape Town visit she is to join Mandela and American actor Bill Cosby for a benefit at Robben Island, where Mandela spent the apartheid years in prison.
She will also speak at the University of Cape Town and attend, with Archbishop Desmond Tutu, a meeting of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission dedicated to resolving apartheid-era crimes.

"South Africa symbolised for all the world the ability to change peacefully, the ability to reconcile the horrors of the past with the hope of the future, the ability to join hands to forge a new and better nation that looks out for all its citizens," she said.
"Now, nearly three years later, South Africa's record of achievement is impressive: economic reform, political reform, a remarkable transformation into a multi-racial democracy," she said.

Mrs. Clinton, on her ninth solo trip outside the United States and the first sitting U.S. first lady to make a goodwill mission to Africa, was also to visit Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Uganda and Eritrea before returning to Washington on March 30.

On Monday in the Senegalese capital of Dakar, she said she hoped to show Americans it was more important than ever to remain engaged with Africa at a time when many nations were holding elections and registering positive economic growth.
"Now is not the time for us to walk away from our commitment to them or our ideals," she told volunteers at a Peace Corps training centre.
